parsed_output.reasoning_summary: This arm is a purely descriptive, jargon-light explainer of how climate science is actually done (weather-station records, satellites, ice cores, volcanic-ash dating, isotopes, OCO-2 precision). Its mechanism is competence/rigor signaling plus vivid effort cues (remote polar stations, deep-sea expeditions), with mild integrity/benevolence content at the end ('inform international assessments... promote sustainable solutions'). Compared with an off-topic filler, this should produce a small-to-moderate lift on the primary multidimensional trust measure (competence and openness subscales moving most), which I center around +3 points — consistent with typical single-exposure informational trust effects of 1–4 points on 0–100 scales. Single-item trust and belief items are anchored on pre-treatment answers, so I shade them lower; distrust is stickier and asymmetric, so I expect a smaller negative. Downstream attitudes (concern, policy support, behavior) are more identity-driven and further along the causal chain, so effects attenuate to roughly a third to a fifth of the trust effect, with the NASA/satellite mention giving institutional trust and research-funding perceptions a slightly larger nudge. Incentivized behaviors (donation, newsletter) should move only trivially, since a single expository text rarely changes costly action.
